title: PERM vs H-1B: What the Green-Card Freeze Means for Indian Tech Workers
excerpt: The US has barred eight major tech and IT-services firms, including Microsoft and TCS, from the labor-certification step of the green-card process. Here's how PERM differs from H-1B and what changes for Indian professionals.
body:
• PERM is not a visa and not a green card. PERM (Program Electronic Review Management) is the Department of Labor's labor-certification step in which a US employer proves no qualified American worker is available for a permanent job. It comes before the I-140 immigrant petition and the green-card application.
  • On October 8, the Trump administration suspended PERM for eight firms — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini. The Department of Labor will not accept new PERM applications or process pending ones involving these companies.
  • Existing H-1B visas are NOT affected by the freeze. India's Ministry of External Affairs clarified on October 9 that PERM is distinct from the H-1B temporary work visa — your H-1B status and your dependents' status remain valid.
  • What this means for you: if you work for one of the eight named employers and were counting on an employer-sponsored green card, your employer's path to sponsor you is blocked for now. Ask your employer's immigration counsel whether a pending PERM filing of yours is frozen, and whether an EB-2 National Interest Waiver — a route that does not require PERM — is viable for you.

Opening: the move that rattled the green-card pipeline

Vice President JD Vance announced on October 8 that the United States would suspend the PERM program for Microsoft. The Department of Labor then named eight companies in total — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini — and said it would stop accepting new PERM applications or processing pending ones involving the suspended firms, accusing them of using the labor-certification system to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

https://x.com/PrabhuChawla/status/2109150504458813630

"Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers."

— JD Vance, Vice President of the United States

What PERM actually is

PERM — Program Electronic Review Management — is a Department of Labor process introduced in 2005 to replace the old paper-based labor-certification system. It is the employer's step, not the worker's: a company sponsoring a foreign employee for permanent residence must first get certification that no qualified American worker is available and that hiring won't depress US wages.

The mechanics run in sequence: the employer defines the permanent role and its requirements, obtains a prevailing wage determination — the Labor Department's benchmark pay for the job and location — then advertises the position to US workers before filing the PERM application (Form ETA-9089) for review.

Certification is only step one: the employer then files an I-140 immigrant petition, and the date the Labor Department accepted the PERM case becomes the worker's priority date — their place in line. For Indians in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories that line is already extraordinarily long, which is why a freeze on new filings matters: it stops the clock from even starting. The green card itself comes last, via I-485 adjustment of status or consular processing.

PERM vs H-1B, side by side

The confusion between the two programs is what has H-1B holders anxious this week. The H-1B is a temporary work visa for foreign professionals in specialty occupations, generally for up to six years. PERM is a labor-certification process tied to permanent employment — one possible step toward an employment-based green card. In short: H-1B is temporary work status, PERM is labor certification for permanent employment, the green card is permanent US residency.

The programs connect because H-1B sponsorship often runs through PERM — but they are legally separate, which is why India's Ministry of External Affairs clarified on October 9 that the suspension "does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents" — though it could affect the permanent-residency process at the suspended companies. The freeze also arrives alongside the administration's proposed $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions, now facing legal challenges, squeezing Indian professionals at both ends: tighter temporary visas and a frozen permanent-residency track.

Diaspora Angle

If you work for one of the eight named employers: (1) your H-1B job and renewals continue normally; (2) your employer's PERM filings are frozen — check with your employer's immigration counsel, not HR rumor, whether your specific case is affected; (3) a priority date locked in from an earlier filing keeps your place in line. The process is documented on the Department of Labor's PERM program page and USCIS's green-card hub.

What's Next

The suspensions stem from what the Labor Department calls ongoing federal investigations, with no end date given. Watch whether more companies are added, how courts rule on the $100,000 H-1B fee proposal, and whether workers pivot to alternatives like the EB-2 National Interest Waiver, which does not require PERM.
